transcript.en: Zainab added up her class's marks with a calculator. Forty numbers, three times, and three different answers! There's a better way. Today: spreadsheets, formulas, and your first lines of Python. A spreadsheet is a big table. Columns have letters: A, B, C. Rows have numbers: one, two, three. So every cell has an address, like B2: column B, row two. A formula starts with an equals sign. SUM of B2 to B9 adds up eight cells: a range. AVERAGE finds the mean, and COUNTIF counts the cells that match. And when a mark changes, the formula updates by itself. No adding up again, and no new mistakes. But it only works if the table is tidy: one value in each cell. Quick check! What does SUM of B2 to B5 add up? B2, B3, B4 and B5: the colon means everything from B2 to B5. That's called a range. Programs can do this too. In Python, a list holds the marks in square brackets. sum adds them up, and len counts them. Divide one by the other, and you have the average. Formulas and programs both need tidy data. A mark typed as fourteen slash seventeen is text, and text can't be added. A Total row inside the data gets counted as a pupil. In the app, Mr Bello's marks sheet gets three questions wrong. Fix the table one tap at a time, and watch the computer's answers turn right. Your turn. Why is a formula better than typing the total yourself? It updates by itself when a mark changes. Remember: every cell has an address, like B2. Formulas start with equals, and work on ranges. And in Python, sum and len do the same job. Try it tomorrow: make a table of something you track for a week, like hours of sleep. Add a total and an average with formulas. Then change one number, and watch them update.

body.en:
A spreadsheet is a big table. Columns have letters (A, B, C) and rows have numbers (1, 2, 3), so every cell has an address: B2 is column B, row 2. A range is a block of cells: B2:B9 means every cell from B2 down to B9.

A formula starts with an equals sign. =SUM(B2:B9) adds up the eight cells in that range. =AVERAGE(B2:B9) finds the mean. =COUNTIF(C2:C9,"6A") counts the cells that say 6A. When a mark changes, every formula updates by itself: no adding up again with a calculator, and no new mistakes.

Programs can do the same job. In Python, a list holds values in square brackets: marks = [14, 9, 17, 12]. sum(marks) adds them up, len(marks) counts them, and sum(marks) / len(marks) is the average. Change a mark in the list, run it again, and you get the new answer.

Formulas and programs both need tidy data: one value in each cell. A mark typed as “14 / 17” is text, and text can’t be added up. A Total row inside the data gets counted as one more pupil. Keep the data tidy, and put totals somewhere else.
body.ar:
جدول البيانات جدول كبير. للأعمدة حروف (A وB وC) وللصفوف أرقام (1 و2 و3)، فلكل خانة عنوان: B2 هي العمود B والصف 2. والنطاق مجموعة من الخانات: B2:B9 تعني كل الخانات من B2 نزولًا إلى B9.

وتبدأ الصيغة بعلامة يساوي. فـ ⁦=SUM(B2:B9)⁩ تجمع الخانات الثماني في هذا النطاق، و⁦=AVERAGE(B2:B9)⁩ تجد المتوسط، و⁦=COUNTIF(C2:C9,"6A")⁩ تعدّ الخانات التي فيها 6A. وحين تتغيّر درجة، تتحدّث كل صيغة وحدها: فلا جمع من جديد بالآلة الحاسبة، ولا أخطاء جديدة.

وتستطيع البرامج أداء العمل نفسه. ففي Python تحمل القائمة قيمًا بين قوسين مربّعين: ⁦marks = [14, 9, 17, 12]⁩. وتجمعها ⁦sum(marks)⁩، وتعدّها ⁦len(marks)⁩، و⁦sum(marks) / len(marks)⁩ هو المتوسط. غيّر درجة في القائمة، وشغّل البرنامج من جديد، فتحصل على الإجابة الجديدة.

وتحتاج الصيغ والبرامج كلتاهما إلى بيانات مرتّبة: قيمة واحدة في كل خانة. فالدرجة المكتوبة «⁦14 / 17⁩» نص، والنص لا يُجمع. وصف المجموع داخل البيانات يُعدّ تلميذًا إضافيًا. فأبقِ البيانات مرتّبة، وضع المجاميع في مكان آخر.

transcript.en: Your class voted online for the school trip. The computer counted “Zoo”, “zoo” and “the zoo” as three different places. It's the same zoo! Today: messy text that breaks counts, and how to clean it. Computers compare text exactly, letter by letter. A space at the end, a capital letter or one different letter makes a new answer. People see one word; the computer sees three. Clean in steps. First, remove the spaces at the ends. Next, make the letters match: all small in English, one form of each Arabic letter. Last, match each answer to a list of allowed answers. Better still, stop it happening. Give people a list to choose from, not a box to type in. A drop-down list means nothing to clean. Quick check! To a computer, is a word with a space at the end the same as the word without it? No: the space is a character too, so it's a different answer. That's why cleaning starts by removing the spaces at the ends. Python can clean text for you. strip removes the spaces at both ends. lower makes every letter small. Do it in a loop, and every answer gets the same treatment. Count again after cleaning. Before: three different places. After: one place, with all nine votes. Same votes, the right answer. In the app, two teachers typed a week's register. Tidy the names, then match them to the class list. Watch the names counted go from twenty to thirteen, and then to eight. Your turn. Which of these stops messy answers before they even start? A drop-down list: nobody types, so nothing gets messy. Remember: computers compare text exactly. Clean in steps: spaces, letters, then a list. And in Python, strip and lower do the tidying. Try it tomorrow: look at a sign-up sheet, or a class poll where people typed their answers. body.en:
Computers compare text exactly, letter by letter. A space at the end, a capital letter or one different letter makes a new answer. So when your class votes for a trip by typing, “Zoo”, “zoo ” and “ZOO” become three different places, even though everyone means the same zoo. Arabic has its own traps: one word can be typed with or without a hamza (أ or ا), with ة or ه at the end, or with ى or ي.

Clean in steps. First, remove the spaces at both ends. Next, make the letters match: all small in English, one form of each Arabic letter. Last, match each answer to a list of allowed answers, so “the zoo” and “Zoo trip” join “zoo” too. Then count again.

Python can do the tidying. strip() removes the spaces at both ends and lower() makes every letter small: " Zoo ".strip().lower() gives "zoo". Do it in a loop, and every answer gets the same treatment. A dictionary can keep the counts: counts[clean] = counts.get(clean, 0) + 1 adds one to that answer’s count.

Better still, stop the mess before it starts. Give people a list to choose from instead of a box to type in. A drop-down list means every answer is written the same way, so there’s nothing to clean.
body.ar:
يقارن الحاسوب النصوص بدقة، حرفًا بحرف. فالمسافة في الآخر، أو الحرف الكبير، أو حرف واحد مختلف، تصنع إجابة جديدة. فحين يصوّت فصلك لرحلة بالكتابة، تصير «Zoo» و«zoo » و«ZOO» ثلاثة أماكن مختلفة، مع أن الجميع يقصد حديقة الحيوان نفسها. وللعربية فخاخها: فالكلمة الواحدة قد تُكتب بهمزة أو دونها (أ أو ا)، أو بـ ة أو ه في آخرها، أو بـ ى أو ي.

نظّف على خطوات. احذف أولًا المسافات من الطرفين. ثم وحّد الحروف: كلها صغيرة في الإنجليزية، وصورة واحدة لكل حرف عربي. وأخيرًا طابِق كل إجابة مع قائمة الإجابات المسموح بها، لتنضم «⁦the zoo⁩» و«⁦Zoo trip⁩» إلى «zoo» أيضًا. ثم عُدّ من جديد.

ويستطيع Python أن يرتّب النصوص. فتحذف ⁦strip()⁩ المسافات من الطرفين، وتجعل ⁦lower()⁩ كل الحروف صغيرة: ⁦" Zoo ".strip().lower()⁩ تعطي ⁦"zoo"⁩. ونفّذ ذلك في حلقة، فتُعامَل كل إجابة المعاملة نفسها. ويستطيع القاموس حفظ الأعداد: ⁦counts[clean] = counts.get(clean, 0) + 1⁩ تضيف واحدًا إلى عدد تلك الإجابة.

والأفضل من ذلك أن تمنع الفوضى قبل أن تبدأ. أعطِ الناس قائمة يختارون منها بدل خانة يكتبون فيها. فالقائمة المنسدلة تعني أن كل إجابة تُكتب بالطريقة نفسها، فلا يبقى ما يُنظَّف.

steps.solution:
votes = ["Zoo", "zoo ", "museum", " Zoo", "farm", "ZOO", "Museum", "zoo"]

for vote in votes:
    clean.append(vote.strip().lower())
print(clean.count("zoo"))
print(clean.count("museum"))

transcript.en: Our weather club's chart showed a flood on Tuesday. It was the sunniest day of the week! One gauge had sent nine nine nine: its code for “I'm broken”. Today: blanks, repeats and impossible values, and how to catch them. Some values are impossible. A mark of twenty-five out of twenty. Rain of nine hundred and ninety-nine millimetres in a day. Minus four pupils. They need checking, not averaging. A blank is not a zero. Zero means we measured, and there was none. Blank means nobody measured. If you turn blanks into zeros, your average becomes a lie. Repeats are the same thing counted twice: one reading, sent two times. Remove the copy, but only when it's really the same station, on the same day. Quick check! A rain gauge reading is blank. What should you write in your report? That one reading is missing. Zero would be a fact you don't have, and the average would be a guess. Say what's missing, and find out why. Python can check every value. Loop through the marks, and count the blanks. Then flag any mark below zero or above twenty. A check is a rule the data must pass. In range: zero to twenty. Not empty. No repeats. When a check fails, set the row aside and ask; don't delete it. In the app, four weather clubs send rain readings. Turn on the checks one by one, and watch the rainfall report change. Turn them all off: suddenly there are six stations! Your turn. A mark says twenty-five, but the test was out of twenty. What do you do? Check it with the teacher: twenty-five out of twenty can't happen. Remember: a blank is not a zero. Look for repeats and impossible values. And when something's wrong, ask; don't guess. Try it tomorrow: check a table you made, or one from class. body.en:
Some values are impossible: a mark of 25 out of 20, 999 mm of rain in one hour, minus four pupils. They aren’t facts; they’re mistakes, or a broken gauge’s error code. Before you use data, ask: could this value really happen? If not, set it aside and ask whoever collected it. Don’t average it, and don’t quietly “fix” it.

A blank is not a zero. Zero means we measured and there was none: zero rain, zero mistakes. Blank means nobody measured. If you turn blanks into zeros, your average becomes a lie, because it includes numbers nobody saw. Leave blanks out of the average, count them, and say how many are missing.

Repeats are the same thing counted twice: one reading sent two times, one pupil typed in twice. Remove the copy, but only when it’s really the same: the same station on the same day, the same pupil in the same test. Two different readings that happen to be equal aren’t repeats.

A check is a rule the data must pass: in range (0 to 20), not empty, no repeats. Python can run checks on every value: loop through the marks, count the blanks (in Python, an empty value is often None), and print any mark below 0 or above 20. Always deal with blanks first: you can’t ask whether nothing is bigger than 20.
body.ar:
بعض القيم مستحيلة: درجة ٢٥ من ٢٠، و٩٩٩ مم من المطر في ساعة واحدة، وسالب أربعة تلاميذ. وهذه ليست حقائق، بل أخطاء، أو رمز خطأ لمقياس معطّل. فقبل أن تستعمل البيانات اسأل: هل يمكن أن تحدث هذه القيمة فعلًا؟ وإن لم يكن، فضعها جانبًا واسأل من جمعها. ولا تحسب متوسطها، ولا «تصلحها» بصمت.

الفراغ ليس صفرًا. فالصفر يعني أننا قسنا ولم نجد شيئًا: صفر مطر، أو صفر أخطاء. أما الفراغ فيعني أن أحدًا لم يقس. وإذا حوّلت الفراغات إلى أصفار صار متوسطك كذبًا، لأنه يضم أعدادًا لم يرها أحد. فاستبعد الفراغات من المتوسط، وعُدّها، وقل كم قيمة ناقصة.

والتكرار هو الشيء نفسه معدودًا مرتين: قراءة واحدة أُرسلت مرتين، أو تلميذ كُتب مرتين. احذف النسخة، لكن فقط حين تكون الشيء نفسه فعلًا: المحطة نفسها في اليوم نفسه، أو التلميذ نفسه في الاختبار نفسه. فقراءتان مختلفتان تتساويان مصادفةً ليستا تكرارًا.

والفحص قاعدة يجب أن تجتازها البيانات: ضمن المدى (من ٠ إلى ٢٠)، وغير فارغة، ودون تكرار. ويستطيع Python أن يطبّق الفحوص على كل قيمة: مرّ على الدرجات بحلقة، وعُدّ الفراغات (والقيمة الفارغة في Python كثيرًا ما تكون None)، واطبع أي درجة أقل من ٠ أو أكبر من ٢٠. وتعامل مع الفراغات أولًا دائمًا: فلا تستطيع أن تسأل هل «لا شيء» أكبر من ٢٠.

transcript.en: An advert says the average customer uses two gigabytes of data a month. Our class checked: most of us use less than one. How can both be true? Today: mean, median and range, and summaries that tell the truth. Here are three ways to sum up numbers. The mean: add them all, and divide by how many. The median: sort them, and take the middle one. The range: the biggest minus the smallest. Five friends' data in a month: one, one, two, three and nine gigabytes. The mean is three point two. The median is two. One heavy user drags the mean up; the median stays put. So which should you use? The mean, when the numbers are similar. The median, when a few are far from the rest, like incomes, house prices or data use. Quick check! Marks of eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, and one typed as one hundred and fifty. Which summary is still about right? The median: thirteen. The mean jumps to forty, which is impossible for marks out of twenty. That's your clue to look for a typo. In Python, sorted puts a list in order. The middle item is the median, and sum divided by len is the mean. Summaries need a chart beside them. Bars start at zero. Give the chart a title, and units on the axis. And say where the data came from. In the app, a week of soil readings with a few glitches. Leave them out, and see which summaries move. The lowest jumps from zero to about fifty-five, but the median doesn't move. Your turn. Which of these makes a bar chart unfair? Bars that don't start at zero make small differences look huge. Remember: the mean adds and divides; the median is the middle. One extreme value drags the mean, not the median. And an honest chart starts at zero. body.en:
There are three common ways to sum up a set of numbers. The mean (the average): add them all and divide by how many there are. The median: sort them, and take the middle one. The range: the biggest minus the smallest. Each tells you something different.

Five friends use 1, 1, 2, 3 and 9 GB of phone data a month. The mean is 16 ÷ 5 = 3.2 GB, but four of the five use less than that! The median is 2 GB: the middle value. One heavy user drags the mean up; the median stays put. That’s how an advert can say “the average customer uses 3.2 GB” while four of these five friends use less.

So which should you use? The mean, when the numbers are similar, like the heights in a class. The median, when a few values are far from the rest, like incomes, house prices or data use, or when one might be a typo. If the mean and the median are far apart, look at the data: something is pulling one of them.

In Python, sum(data) / len(data) is the mean, and sorted(data) puts the list in order, so the middle item is the median. And a summary needs a chart beside it: bars start at zero, the chart has a title and units, and you say where the data came from.

هناك ثلاث طرق شائعة لتلخيص مجموعة من الأعداد. المتوسط: اجمعها كلها واقسم على عددها. والوسيط: رتّبها وخذ الوسطى. والمدى: الأكبر ناقص الأصغر. وكلٌّ منها يخبرك بشيء مختلف.

يستهلك خمسة أصدقاء ١ و١ و٢ و٣ و٩ غيغابايت من بيانات الهاتف في الشهر. المتوسط ١٦ ÷ ٥ = ٣٫٢ غيغابايت، لكن أربعة من الخمسة يستهلكون أقل من ذلك! والوسيط ٢ غيغابايت: القيمة الوسطى. فمستخدم واحد كثير الاستهلاك يشدّ المتوسط إلى أعلى، أما الوسيط فيبقى مكانه. وهكذا يستطيع إعلان أن يقول «الزبون المتوسط يستهلك ٣٫٢ غيغابايت» بينما يستهلك أربعة من هؤلاء الأصدقاء الخمسة أقل من ذلك.

فأيّهما تستعمل؟ المتوسط حين تتقارب الأعداد، كأطوال التلاميذ في فصل. والوسيط حين تبتعد بعض القيم عن غيرها، كالدخل أو أسعار البيوت أو استهلاك البيانات، أو حين قد تكون إحداها خطأً في الكتابة. وإذا تباعد المتوسط عن الوسيط، فانظر في البيانات: هناك ما يشدّ أحدهما.

وفي Python يكون ⁦sum(data) / len(data)⁩ هو المتوسط، وترتّب ⁦sorted(data)⁩ القائمة، فيكون العنصر الأوسط هو الوسيط. والملخّص يحتاج إلى رسم بجانبه: أعمدة تبدأ من الصفر، وعنوان ووحدات للرسم، وذكر مصدر البيانات.

en: Teams (2 min): Make teams of four and give each team a sheet of paper for its answers.
Quiz (15 min): Read each question aloud; each team agrees on one answer and writes it down.
Explain (8 min): Reveal each answer and ask one team to explain why it’s right.
ar: الفرق (دقيقتان): كوّنوا فرقًا من أربعة، وأعطِ كل فريق ورقة لإجاباته.

الشرح (٨ دقائق): اكشف كل إجابة، واطلب من أحد الفرق أن يشرح سبب صحّتها.
